senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: positive moral qualities of the most general nature
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no abstract term such as ‘goodness.’ Since goodness implies some type of activity involving others, one must frequently use a verb expression, for example, ‘to be good to’ or ‘to benefit.’ The qualification ‘full of’ in Romans 15:14 must likewise be restructured in a number of languages so as to indicate the fact that one always engages in doing good, for example, ‘that you are always doing good to people.’

senses.def: pertaining to having the proper characteristics or performing the expected function in a fully satisfactory way
pertaining to being generous, with the implication of its relationship to goodness
(pl) possessions which provide material benefits, usually used with reference to movable or storable possessions rather than real estate
senses.comment: It may also be possible to translate Luke 12:19 as ‘you have all you need to live well for many years.’

senses.def: pertaining to not being perceived
senses.comment: Though in Greek ἄδηλος may designate anything which is unperceived by any of the senses, in Luke 11:44 the most evident sense involved would be sight, and therefore one may translate ‘because you are like graves that cannot be seen.’

senses.def: to have the capacity to perceive clearly and hence to understand the real nature of something
glosses: to have the capacity to understand

senses.def: to make a loud, reverberating sound
to cry or weep intensely and with wailing
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ἀλαλάζω[b] is a term or phrase referring to ritual or ceremonial weeping or wailing. This would not necessarily imply lack of sincerity, but it would be typical of what would frequently occur in many societies in the case of the type of presumed death reported in Mark 5:38.

senses.def: pertaining to that which does not change from one state to another
to get rid of someone by execution, often with legal or quasi-legal procedures
to speak with considerable volume or loudness
(derivative of ἀνταλλάσσω ‘to exchange,’ not occurring in the NT) that which is exchanged or given in exchange

senses.subdomain: Once, Twice, Three Times, Etc. [Cardinals of Time]
senses.def: a single occurrence

senses.subdomain: Once, Twice, Three Times, Etc. [Cardinals of Time]
senses.def: a single occurrence to the exclusion of any other similar occurrence
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘once and for all’ is simply ‘once and not again’ or ‘once and not twice.’

senses.subdomain: Once, Twice, Three Times, Etc. [Cardinals of Time]
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: once and twice) an indefinite low number, but more than once
to crowd in hard against

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἀποτομία ‘to show harshness,’ 88.73) pertaining to acting or dealing harshly with someone
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ἀποτομία (88.73) or ἀποτόμως is a negative expression combined with showing kindness, and therefore one may translate ‘to refuse to show kindness.’ In a number of circumstances, however, the equivalent of ἀποτομία or ἀποτόμως is a highly idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to refuse to look at,’ ‘to frown upon,’ or ‘to push aside.’

senses.def: to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
senses.comment: This interpretation of Philippians 2:6 reflects the position of Jesus after the incarnation and the fact that he had no thought of trying to become equal with God because he already possessed all of the qualities of deity. Some traditional translations have rendered the latter part of Philippians 2:6 as ‘did not think it robbery to be equal with God,’ but see 57.236.

senses.def: that which is to be held on to forcibly
senses.comment: Compare the rendering of ἁρπαγμός[a] in 57.235. Since ἁρπαγμός may mean not only ‘to grasp something forcefully which one does not have’ (57.235) but also ‘to retain by force what one possesses,’ it is possible to translate Philippians 2:6 in two quite different ways. This second interpretation of ἁρπαγμός presumes the position of Jesus prior to the incarnation and hence his willingness to experience the kenosis or ‘emptying’ of his divine prerogatives. In any translation of Philippians 2:6 it is important that both possible renderings be clearly indicated, one in the text and the other in the margin.

senses.def: a city of Mysia
to destroy the value or use of something
to cause something to be unattractive or unsightly
to become such as not to be seen
glosses: to become invisible (in the passive, to disappear, to vanish)
senses.comment: In a number of instances one can best render ‘vanishes’ as ‘cannot be seen’ or ‘suddenly people cannot see it.’

senses.def: to cease to exist, with the implication of no longer being evident or visible

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a person not participating in Greek culture and civilization (βάρβαρος contrasts with Ἕλλην[a] ‘Greek,’ 11.90, with the focus on culture rather than on language; see 1 Corinthians 14:11 at 11.94)
senses.comment: It would be a mistake in the case of Romans 1:14 to speak merely of ‘Greeks and barbarians’ or ‘Greeks and savages.’ By NT times Ἕλλην (see 11.90) would have included most of those who participated in one way or another in the culture of the Greco-Roman world. Accordingly, one may render the contrast in Romans 1:14 as ‘the civilized and the uncivilized.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: the native people of an area in which a language other than Greek or Latin was spoken (such persons would be regarded as being outside the civilized world of NT times)
senses.comment: In rendering this expression in Acts 28:2 it would be possible in some languages to translate ‘the people there who spoke a strange language were friendly to us’ or ‘the local inhabitants of that island were kind to us.’ ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος καὶ ὁ λαλῶν ἐν ἐμοὶ βάρβαρος ‘I will be a foreigner to the one who speaks, and the one who speaks will be a foreigner to me’ 1 Corinthians 14:11. In 1 Corinthians 14:11 βάρβαρος implies being a foreigner from a country outside of the so-called civilized world.

senses.def: a pattern of behavior associated with a low cultural level
senses.comment: Regardless of the level of culture or civilization, each ethnic group seems to be able to point to some other group regarded as being uncivilized. In some languages such a group is identified as ‘those who live far away’ or ‘those who do not live in towns’ or ‘those who are very strange.’ In Colossians 3:11 Σκύθης ‘Scythian’ (93.583) may represent a state of civilization even lower than that implied by βάρβαρος ‘barbarian.’

senses.def: to experience a violent attack
senses.comment: In many languages it may be difficult, if not impossible, to speak of the kingdom of heaven ‘suffering violent attacks,’ but generally some active form may be employed, for example, ‘and violently attack the kingdom of heaven’ or ‘ … the rule of God.’ See comment at βιάζω[b] 20.10.

senses.def: to employ violence in doing harm to someone or something
senses.comment: Since there are a number of different interpretations of this expression (πᾶς εἰς αὐτὴν βιάζεται) in Luke 16:16 as well as for the parallel expression in Matthew 11:12 (ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν βιάζεται; see βιάζω[a]); it is important to consult various commentaries before undertaking a translation. Probably the most widely held interpretation of these difficult expressions is based on the fact that many people did not hesitate to employ violence or military force in order to establish what they regarded as the rule of God on earth.

senses.def: to consume solid food
a meal whether simple or elaborate
senses.comment: Though ἄριστον[a], δεῖπνον[a], and βρῶσις[b] are highly generic in this usage, it is not necessary to translate these terms by a corresponding generic term in another language, since a more specific term may fit the context more satisfactorily. In fact, a generic term might be quite inappropriate in that it would suggest in the case of Mark 6:21 that Herod was quite stingy in simply providing an ordinary meal for his officials.

senses.def: any kind of food or nourishment
senses.comment: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as Matthew 6:11 as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering Luke 4:4 (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of Luke 4:4 is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

senses.def: any type of solid food, particularly meat
the process of producing rust or tarnish by oxidation
senses.comment: Though in Matthew 6:19 βρῶσις has been generally understood to mean ‘corrosion,’ it might actually refer to a type of insect, as it does in the Septuagint of Malachi 3.11.

senses.def: the surface of the earth as the dwelling place of mankind, in contrast with the heavens above and the world below

senses.subdomain: Land in Contrast With the Sea
senses.def: dry land, in contrast with the sea
senses.comment: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between terms which designate land in contrast with water and those which designate cultivated land. Even in English the normal term for land close to water is ‘shore’ or ‘coast,’ and therefore one may translate Matthew 14:24 as ‘the boat was already far away from the shore.’ Similarly, in Acts 27:27 one may translate ‘we were getting close to shore.’

senses.def: the loose top layer of earth in which plants grow, usually black, brown, or reddish in color and made of organic matter and mineral particles
senses.comment: The meaning of γῆ[c] may be expressed in some instances as soil for planting or ground for plants.

senses.def: region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration
glosses: land (and even district, though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)
senses.comment: The meanings of γῆ[d], χώρα[b], κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος[c] are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of γῆ[a] ‘earth,’ 1.39) all people who dwell on the earth
a more or less fixed phrase: the heavens and the earth, equivalent to a single lexical item: the totality of God’s creation
senses.comment: There may be certain complications involved in rendering ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ as ‘heaven and earth,’ since ‘heaven’ might be interpreted in some languages as referring only to the dwelling place of God himself. The referents in this passage are ‘the sky and the earth,’ in other words, all of physical existence, but not the dwelling place of God, for the latter would not be included in what is destined to pass away.

senses.def: to lend money, normally with the expectation of receiving the same amount in return plus interest
senses.comment: In Luke 6:34 it is possible that no interest payment is involved, in which case the meaning is similar to that of κίχρημι ‘to lend’ (57.214).

senses.def: to borrow money, normally with the implication of interest to be paid
senses.comment: It is possible, however, that in Matthew 5:42 interest on the loan is not involved.

senses.def: pertaining to being able to be known by the public
senses.comment: The rendering of διακατηλέγχετο in Acts 18:28 provides the verbal correspondences ‘he … refuted … in … debate.’ The term δημοσίᾳ indicates that the debates took place in public so that everyone could know or did know what was said and proven. It is, of course, possible to understand δημοσίᾳ only in the sense of ‘public setting,’ but in Acts 18:28 something more than mere setting seems to be implied.

senses.def: to plunder something thoroughly or completely
senses.comment: In some languages one may render ‘plunder’ as ‘to carry off all that one can.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being right as the result of being justified and deserved
a Greek silver coin with approximately the same value as the denarius

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to exercise complete control over one’s desires and actions
senses.comment: An adequate rendering of the expression ‘to exercise self-control’ may require an idiomatic equivalent, for example, ‘to hold oneself in,’ ‘to command oneself,’ ‘to be a chief of oneself,’ ‘to make one’s heart be obedient,’ ‘to command one’s own desires,’ ‘to be the master of what one wants,’ or ‘to say No to one’s body.’ (Compare ἀκρασία ‘lack of self-control,’ 88.91, and ἀκρατής ‘lacking in self-control,’ 88.92.)

senses.subdomain: Double, Four Times As Much, Etc. [Multiples]
senses.def: one hundred times as much in quantity

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
senses.def: the totality of a period of time, with the implication of proper completion
to cause something to be in the shape of a roll
to cause to be made known, with possible emphasis upon the means
to do something to someone, normally with the implication of something bad or unfortunate
to cut or incise letters or designs
to celebrate a festival or feast
possessing more or less definite information about, possibly with a degree of thoroughness or competence
senses.comment: It is also possible to render ἐπίγνωσις in Romans 1:28 as ‘true knowledge.’ For another interpretation of ἐπίγνωσις as part of an idiom in Romans 1:28, see 31.28.

senses.def: the content of what is definitely known
(an idiom, literally: to come into knowledge) to acquire information about something, with emphasis upon the process involved
senses.comment: It is also possible to treat the phrase εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἔρχομαι as meaning ‘to come to know’ in the sense of ‘to come to understand’ (see 32.17).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to come into knowledge) to come to understand the meaning of something, with special emphasis upon the process
senses.comment: One may also interpret εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἔρχομαι as meaning ‘to come to have knowledge of, to come to know’ (see 27.4).

senses.def: the coming of divine power, either for benefit or judgment
senses.comment: In 1 Peter 2:12 the reference may be to God’s coming to rule or his coming in judgment.

senses.def: a religious role involving both service and leadership
senses.comment: See discussion at 53.71. For a more probable interpretation of ἐπισκοπή in Acts 1:20, see 35.40.

senses.def: (derivative of ἐπισκοπέω[a] ‘to take care of,’ 35.39) the position of one who has responsibility for the care of someone
senses.comment: Though in some contexts ἐπισκοπή has been regarded traditionally as a position of authority, in reality the focus is upon the responsibility for caring for others, and in the context of Acts 1:20 the reference is clearly to the responsibility for caring for the church (see 53.69).

senses.def: suffering destruction, with the implication of being deserted and abandoned

(a fixed phrase derived from Hebrew, literally: the detestable thing of desolation) an abomination (either an object or an event) which defiles a holy place and thus causes it to be abandoned and left desolate
senses.comment: In translating βδέλυγμα, it may be necessary in some languages to use a phrase such as ‘that which God detests’ or ‘that which God hates’ or even ‘that which causes God’s anger.’ The term ἐρημώσεως may then be translated as ‘that which causes people to abandon’ or ‘that which causes something to be deserted.’ The entire phrase may then be translated in some languages as ‘that which God detests and which causes something to be abandoned’ or ‘… left desolate.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the quality of uprightness
senses.comment: In a number of languages it makes no sense to speak of a ‘righteous scepter,’ and therefore this expression in Hebrews 1:8 may be better rendered as ‘you will rule righteously’ or ‘the way in which you rule is just.’

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: one who thinks up schemes or plans of action

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Binding and Fastening
senses.def: a thin piece of metal (usually iron) sharpened on one end (in the NT used only in connection with nails employed in the crucifixion)
senses.comment: In a number of languages a distinction is made between relatively small nails and larger spikes; the latter would be appropriate in speaking of crucifixion.

senses.def: appropriate beliefs and devout practice of obligations relating to supernatural persons and powers
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no specific term equivalent to ‘religion,’ but one may always speak of this phase of culture by some phrase such as ‘how to act toward God’ or ‘what one does to placate spirits’ or ‘how one worships.’

senses.def: any type of altar or object where gifts may be placed and ritual observances carried out in honor of supernatural beings (in the NT θυσιαστήριον is employed to refer to a number of different types of altars; including the altar for burnt offerings in the Temple; the altar of incense; the altar which Abraham built; and the heavenly altar mentioned in the book of Revelation)
senses.comment: A descriptive equivalent of ‘altar’ occurs in some languages as ‘a place where offerings are made to God’ or ‘a place where gifts are given to God.’ In some contexts it may be necessary to add phrases such as ‘where sacrifices are burned to God’ or ‘where incense is burned to honor God.’

senses.def: the southern part of Palestine
the wider region (beyond the southern part of Palestine) occupied by the Jewish nation
to cause something to become clean
senses.comment: In John 15:2 the meaning of καθαίρω may also be understood as ‘to prune branches’ (see 43.12), thus playing on two distinct meanings of καθαίρω.

senses.def: to cut away or cut back unproductive branches or to cut back productive branches so they can produce better

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to a positive moral quality, with the implication of being favorably valued
pertaining to events which measure up to their intended purpose
senses.comment: In the 65.23 contexts, βελτίων, καλῶς[b], εὖ[b], and εὖγε occur in highly elliptical constructions.

senses.def: pertaining to being accurate and right, with a possible implication of being commendable

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: pertaining to having high status, with the possible implication of its attractiveness
senses.comment: It is also possible that καλῶς in James 2:3 has the meaning of a polite invitation, translatable as ‘please!’ (see 33.177).

senses.def: a marker of polite request
senses.comment: For another interpretation of καλῶς in James 2:3, see 87.25.

senses.def: a positive degree (and even more emphatic in the comparative form κάλλιον) with an implication of correctness
(an idiom, literally: to have well) the state of being healthy, well (in contrast with sickness)
senses.comment: In a number of languages health is expressed only in terms of strength, for ‘to be well’ is ‘to be strong.’ In other languages, however, to be well or to be healthy is a negation of illness or sickness, so that in Mark 16:18 one may translate ‘they will place their hands on those who are sick and these people will become not sick.’

senses.def: to judge someone as definitely guilty and thus subject to punishment
glosses: to render a verdict of guilt

senses.def: to have or possess objects or property (in the technical sense of having control over the use of such objects)
the act of taking possession of something
to take away the power or significance of something
glosses: to cause to be emptied of power

senses.subdomain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
senses.def: to completely remove or eliminate elements of high status or rank by eliminating all privileges or prerogatives associated with such status or rank

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of κληρόω ‘to be chosen by lot,’ not occurring in the NT) to choose, with the implication of supernatural or divine intervention or guidance
glosses: to choose in accordance with the will of God

senses.def: a city in Greece
a position completely encircling an area or object
to serve, with the implication of more formal or regular service
to perform religious rites as part of one’s religious duties or as the result of one’s role
pertaining to the language spoken in Lycaonia
to acquire information as the result of instruction, whether in an informal or formal context
to learn from experience, often with the implication of reflection
to come to understand as the result of a process of learning
senses.comment: It is possible to understand μανθάνω in 1 Corinthians 4:6 as meaning simply ‘to learn’ (see 27.12).

senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

senses.subdomain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About
senses.def: a negative reference to an entity, event, or state
senses.comment: Though in English one may readily say ‘tell no one’ or ‘take nothing,’ in a number of languages the negation must be related to the verb and not to a pronominal object. Accordingly, it may be necessary to translate as ‘do not tell anyone’ or ‘do not take anything.’

senses.def: pertaining to one who has only one eye with which he can see (in other words, one who is blind in one eye)
visible mass of particles of water in the sky; varies in color from white to dark grey; source of rain
senses.comment: In many languages it would be difficult to speak of ‘a cloud coming up in the west,’ for this would seem to imply that a cloud was actually rising from below the earth. In some languages it is better to speak of ‘a cloud getting larger’ or, in the specific context of Luke 12:54, one may translate ‘when you see a cloud coming to you from the west.’

senses.def: to pierce with a pointed instrument; normally not as serious a wound as is implied by ἐκκεντέω ‘to pierce,’ 19.14
pertaining to being similar to something else in some respect
interrogative references to class or kind
senses.comment: This meaning is also found as a variant reading: ὑγιὴς ἐγίνετο οἵῳ δήποτ οὖν κατείχετο νοσήματι ‘was made well from whatever disease he had’ John 5:3 (apparatus).

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὁπλίζομαι ‘to arm oneself,’ not occurring in the NT) to prepare, with focus upon the process of equipping
combination of the negative particle οὐ[a] ‘not,’ 69.3, and the postpositive conjunction δέ[a] ‘and,’ 89.94
combination of the negative particle οὐ[a] 69.3, and the postpositional particle δέ ‘even,’ which does not occur with this sense as an independent graphic unit in the NT
a province in the southern part of Asia Minor
to rebel, with the implication of provoking to anger
glosses: to rebel and provoke to anger

senses.def: the totality of any object, mass, collective, or extension
any one of a totality
a degree of totality or completeness
(with the definite article) pertaining to being entire or whole, with focus on the totality
a totality of kinds or sorts

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: through all) a number of related points of time, occurring at regular intervals

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: through all) duration of time, either continuous or episodic, but without limits
senses.comment: In some languages there may be problems involved in rendering ἀεί or διὰ παντός[b], since there may be a basic distinction between (a) continuous activity and (b) activity which may be defined as episodic in that it regularly recurs in related episodes. For example, in 2 Corinthians 6:10 the fact of being glad may be related specifically to the occasions of being saddened, while in Matthew 18:10 the focus of meaning is probably upon the continuous nature of the relation.

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: clothing as a covering

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: any type of outer garment
senses.comment: The choice of an equivalent for these terms relating to ‘outer garments’ will depend largely upon the specific context and the usage in each receptor language. The most common equivalent is a term meaning ‘coat.’

senses.def: a bag used by travellers (or beggars) to carry possessions
senses.comment: It is possible that in Matthew 10:10 (and parallel passages) the reference is specifically to a ‘beggar’s bag’ used to collect food or money.

senses.def: to have considerably more than what would be regarded as the norm in a society
to prosper to the point of being rich
senses.comment: In some instances it may be useful to translate ‘to become wealthy’ as ‘he soon possessed much’ or even ‘he was no longer poor, but rich.’ By introducing ‘poor’ in contrast with ‘rich,’ one may identify a change of state.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πλουτέω[b] ‘to become rich,’ 57.28) to give generously of one’s wealth
to have a large amount of something which has value
glosses: to have a great deal of

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: a number of related points of time, occurring in interrogative or exclamatory contexts
to continue to move forward

senses.subdomain: Pass, Cross Over, Go Through, Go Around
senses.def: to move continuously along a particular path or route
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ῥύμην μίαν in Acts 12:10 as referring to a particular section or block in a street; therefore, one may translate ‘they went one street further.’

senses.def: to come/go prior to some other event, normally one involving a similar type of movement
senses.comment: Though the movement referred to by φθάνω[b] and προέρχομαι[c] may involve movement which is spacially ahead of someone else, nevertheless the focus of meaning is not a spacial relationship but a temporal one.

senses.def: to go in front of, in order to show the way

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a Gentile who had converted to Judaism
the back part of a boat
senses.comment: See translation suggestion at 6.46.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to violate moral principles by acting in an unscrupulous manner
senses.comment: ῥᾳδιουργία and ῥᾳδιούργημα may often be rendered simply as ‘doing what one should not do.’ These terms also may often be translated merely as ‘cheating.’

senses.def: a place of which Melchizedek was king; see also 93.321
the expression βασιλεὺς Σαλήμ ‘king of Salem’ (Hebrews 7:1 may be interpreted as ‘king of peace,’ and as such it may be regarded as an honorific name
senses.comment: It is also possible that Σαλήμ refers to a place (see 93.566).

senses.def: pertaining to that which has been damaged by the larvae of moths
senses.comment: This expression in James 5:2 may often be rendered as ‘your garments have been eaten by worms’ or ‘your garments are full of holes.’

senses.def: (derivative of Σκυθία ‘Scythia,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who is a native of Scythia, a region north of the Black Sea, and regarded by the GrecoRoman world as utterly pagan and uncivilized
a wreath of wool to which leaves and flowers might be added and either wound around a staff or woven into a garland to be worn on the head
senses.comment: Garlands were an important part of the ritual involved in the worship of pagan gods in the ancient world. Such a garland may be described as ‘a circle of leaves’ or ‘a ring of flowers’ or ‘a wreath of flowers.’

senses.def: to cause parts to fit together in an overall arrangement
one who is an elder along with others

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: a person who is of one’s own age
(derivative of σχίζω[a] ‘to split, to tear,’ 19.27) the condition resulting from the splitting or tearing
senses.comment: The separation indicated by σχίσμα[a] may be quite different in some languages, depending upon the substance involved, for example, cloth, leather, paper, and clouds.

senses.def: a division into opposing groups, generally two
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘causing division’ is literally ‘to cause two groups in place of one group,’ but more frequently the equivalent is expressed in terms of attitudes, for example, ‘to cause people to be angry at one another’ or ‘to cause people not to like one another’ or ‘to cause people to think of one another as enemies.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: maturity in thought and behavior

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a state of perfection, implying some process of maturity
to be so bold as to challenge or defy possible danger or opposition
(derivative of Τύρος ‘Tyre,’ 93.602) a person who lives in or is a native of Tyre
an extraordinary degree, involving a considerable excess over what would be expected (this series differs from the series in 78.31 primarily in emphasizing the excessive degree)
the measurement of height
senses.comment: In Ephesians 3:18 the four different dimensions of space are used figuratively in the sense of ‘that which is all-encompassing.’

senses.def: a location above the earth and associated with supernatural events or beings
senses.comment: In Luke 24:49 ὕψος refers to heaven as a type of substitute reference for God, and in many languages it is advisable to translate ‘until the power from God comes down on you.’ In Ephesians 4:8 the phrase ἀναβὰς εἰς ὕψος may be rendered literally as ‘when he went up to the heights,’ but it is preferable in a number of languages to translate ‘when he went up to heaven,’ for a literal rendering of ‘heights’ might imply only a high building or a mountain.|In contexts in which these expressions refer clearly to ‘heaven’ or ‘the sky,’ it is better to use terms meaning ‘heaven’ or ‘sky’ rather than terms meaning ‘height’ or ‘that which is high.’

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a position of high status
(an idiom, literally: dawning from on high) the bright dawn of salvation (or possibly to be understood as a title for the Messiah)
senses.comment: The expression ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους occurs in a highly poetic liturgical passage in Luke 1, and many translators have preferred to retain the more or less literal rendering. Others, however, have interpreted this as the dawning of salvation and have therefore translated ἐπισκέψεται ἡμᾶς ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους as ‘salvation will dawn upon us from heaven’ or ‘from heaven salvation will come to us as the dawn does.’ If one wishes to employ ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους as simply a title for the Messiah, one can translate ‘the Messiah will come to us,’ but it is normally better to preserve the figurative expression and relate it to the coming of the Messiah as ‘the Messiah will come to us even as the dawn does from on high.’ One may also treat the problem of interpretation in a footnote.

senses.def: one of the twelve apostles
a son of Herod the Great and brother of Herod Antipas

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: a subgroup of a nation which is regarded as being more closely related biologically than the entire nation
senses.comment: In a number of societies there are only three well-defined biologically related groups: (1) the nuclear family (that is to say, the immediate family); (2) the extended family (often referred to as ‘the clan’); and (3) the tribe or nation as a whole. Under such circumstances it may be necessary to speak of the twelve tribes of Israel as being ‘twelve large clans.’ This would emphasize their biological relationships and at the same time would suggest that they constituted part of a larger ethnic unit, namely, the nation. On the other hand, a number of so-called ‘primitive societies’ have a great many designations for different sets of biologically related persons. These may designate an individual family, an extended family, the clan, a grouping of clans, a division of a tribe into two interacting units (called moieties), and finally the tribe as a whole, equivalent in larger societies to a nation. The choice of appropriate terms for various groups of biologically related persons becomes particularly complex in certain passages in the OT.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a relatively large unit of people who constitute a sociopolitical group, sharing a presumed biological descent (in many contexts πατριά[b] and φυλή[b] are very similar in meaning to ἔθνος[a], 11.55)

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (a set phrase, literally: the twelve tribes, but used in a figurative sense) all of the people of God as a possible reference to the new Israel
senses.comment: It is possible to understand James 1:1 as containing a salutation to the twelve tribes of Israel scattered throughout the Diaspora, but this literal interpretation has generally been rejected for a reference to all of God’s people scattered throughout the known world. If one elects to follow a literal translation of this passage, it would be important to introduce a marginal note indicating the alternative meaning and vice versa.

senses.def: an island, with a city of the same name, in the Aegean Sea
to communicate what is false, with the evident purpose of misleading
senses.comment: The Greek term ψεύδομαι and the English equivalent ‘to lie’ involve more than simply telling what is not true, for this could occur without an intent to deceive or mislead. ψεύδομαι, therefore, involves not only the communication of a falsehood but also the intent to deceive.
